# Amazon EC2: say it

<!-- speak:start id=ec2-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** The instance is at 9% most of the day. Are we paying for a size that we do not need?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Probably yes. The instance is bigger than the work needs. A smaller size that can burst for the morning peak costs less.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is yes, you are probably paying for unused capacity.

It works like this. An instance is the virtual computer that you rent from AWS.

When it is bigger than the work, you pay for idle power.

AWS Compute Optimizer reads your usage and says when a smaller size still meets the need.

Your use is low most of the day, with a short peak in the morning.

For that shape, a burstable instance fits. It earns credits in quiet hours and spends them in the peak.

The thing to watch is the change itself. You have to stop the instance to change its size.

And the morning peak must still fit in the new size.

In your case, I'd move the web part to a smaller burstable instance.

Can we take a short maintenance window on a weekday night?

**Skeleton.** yes, the size is too big / Compute Optimizer compares use and size / burstable earns credits, spends in peak / resize needs a stop

**Must say.**

- An instance is over-provisioned when it can be sized down and still meet the performance requirements, and over-provisioning leads to extra costs.
- AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes the instance specifications and utilization metrics, and recommends changes to improve performance, save money, or both.
- A burstable instance earns CPU credits while it stays below its baseline and spends them when it bursts above the baseline.
- You must stop an EBS-backed instance before you change its instance type, so you plan for downtime.

**Do not say.**

- "AWS changes the size while the instance keeps running". Say: You must stop an EBS-backed instance before you change its instance type, so plan a short downtime.
- "after the change the morning peak no longer matters". Say: Under-provisioning can result in poor performance. The new size still has to handle the morning peak.
- "a burstable instance can run at full CPU all day for the same price". Say: If a workload consistently requires CPU usage much higher than the baseline, AWS suggests dedicated CPU instances such as M or C.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Do we pay extra if the morning peak goes above the baseline? In unlimited mode, the hourly price covers the spikes if the average stays at or below the baseline over a rolling 24-hour period. Above that, you pay a flat additional rate per vCPU-hour.
- Should we buy a Savings Plan first, to get the discount now? Right-size first. Oversized instances waste money under any purchasing model, so a commitment on the large size keeps paying for the waste.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=ec2-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Should we buy a Savings Plan, or run everything on Spot to save money?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both lower the price, but for different work. Use a Savings Plan for the steady base, and Spot only for work that can restart.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both lower your bill, but they fit different kinds of work.

It works like this. With a Savings Plan, you commit to steady use for a long term.

It pays off for work that runs all the time, like your database.

Spot uses spare AWS capacity at a big discount.

But Amazon EC2 can take it back with two minutes of notice.

So Spot fits stateless work that can stop and restart, like batch jobs.

The thing to watch is this. Never put the database or a hard deadline on Spot.

And a Savings Plan gives a discount, not reserved capacity.

In your case, mix them. Put the steady base on a Savings Plan, and restartable jobs on Spot.

Which of your jobs can restart if an instance disappears?

**Skeleton.** both cut cost, different work / Savings Plan for steady base / Spot can leave in two minutes / not the database, no capacity

**Must say.**

- Steady workloads with consistent, predictable use, such as databases, benefit most from long-term commitments through Savings Plans.
- Amazon EC2 can interrupt a Spot Instance, with two minutes of notice, when it needs the capacity back.
- Spot suits stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications, and does not suit inflexible, stateful or fault-intolerant work.
- Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation; an On-Demand Capacity Reservation holds capacity.

**Do not say.**

- "Spot is fine for the database too". Say: Spot Instances are not suitable for inflexible, stateful or fault-intolerant workloads. Put the database on steady capacity.
- "a Savings Plan guarantees our capacity". Say: Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation. Use an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for that.
- "the Savings Plan discount also applies to our Spot Instances". Say: Spot Instances are not covered by Savings Plans.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Do we get a warning before a Spot Instance goes away? Yes. Amazon EC2 gives two minutes of notice. The notice arrives as an EventBridge event and as items in the instance metadata, so your job can save its work.
- Does our Savings Plan make Spot cheaper as well? No. Spot Instances are not covered by Savings Plans, and Spot spend does not count toward a Compute Savings Plans commitment.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Our engineers SSH into production servers from home. How do we close port 22 and still fix things?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Use Session Manager. Engineers get a shell with no open inbound port, no bastion host and no SSH keys.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: use Session Manager, a part of AWS Systems Manager.

It works like this. Each instance gets an IAM role with one AWS managed policy.

The policy is called Amazon SSM Managed Instance Core.

Engineers then open a shell on the instance through Session Manager.

There's no inbound rule, no bastion host, and no SSH key to manage.

The agent connects out over HTTPS, through VPC endpoints or outbound internet access.

So you can delete the SSH rule from the security group.

The thing to watch is the role. Without it, Session Manager usually can't connect.

In your case, try it on one test instance first, then on production.

Does anyone need a real SSH client, for example to copy files?

**Skeleton.** Session Manager, no open port / role and an outbound path / delete the SSH rule / no role, no connection

**Must say.**

- Session Manager gives access without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
- The instance must be managed by Systems Manager and have an attached IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy.
- Security group rules should not permit access on port 22/tcp (SSH) or port 3389/tcp (RDP); use Session Manager for interactive access.
- The SSM Agent starts every connection. Without VPC endpoints, the instance needs outbound internet access and HTTPS outbound to Systems Manager.

**Do not say.**

- "restrict the SSH port to the office IP address and you are done". Say: Security group rules should not permit access on port 22/tcp (SSH). Use Session Manager for interactive access.
- "you need a bastion host in a public subnet". Say: Session Manager works without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys.
- "store an access key on the instance for the agent". Say: Use an IAM role. Its credentials are temporary, and AWS rotates them automatically.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Some engineers need a real SSH client. What then? Use EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint. It connects without a bastion host, and the instance does not need a public IP address.
- Can we see later what an engineer did in a session? Yes. Well-Architected advises Session Manager for interactive access, with session logging to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** Our service loads a large model into memory for 20 minutes every morning. Can we switch the servers off at night without that wait?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Yes, if the instances are launched with hibernation turned on. At night the memory is saved to the encrypted root volume.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is yes: hibernate the instances instead of stopping them.

It works like this. Hibernation saves the memory to the EBS root volume.

When the instance starts again, the memory is loaded back, so the model is already there.

At night you pay for the disk storage, not for instance usage.

The thing to watch is the setup. You turn hibernation on only when you launch the instance.

The root volume must be encrypted EBS.

On Linux, the memory must be one hundred fifty gibibytes or less.

And instances in an Auto Scaling group can't hibernate.

In your case, check the memory size first.

How much memory does each instance have, and are they in an Auto Scaling group?

**Skeleton.** hibernate, memory to root volume / pay storage, not instance / turn on at launch, encrypted EBS / memory limit, no Auto Scaling

**Must say.**

- Hibernation saves the RAM contents to the EBS root volume and reloads them when the instance starts, so a slow-to-start application returns to service sooner.
- You turn on hibernation when you launch the instance; you cannot turn it on for an existing instance.
- The root volume must be an encrypted EBS volume, and a Linux instance cannot hibernate with more than 150 GiB of RAM.
- A hibernated instance has no instance usage fee; you pay standard EBS storage rates and any Elastic IP addresses.

**Do not say.**

- "we can turn hibernation on for the running instances tonight". Say: You can't enable hibernation on an existing instance. Turn it on when you launch the new instances.
- "we pay nothing while they hibernate". Say: A hibernated instance is charged at standard EBS rates for storage, and Elastic IP addresses are still charged.
- "any instance size can hibernate". Say: A Linux instance cannot hibernate with more than 150 GiB of RAM, and a Windows instance cannot with more than 16 GiB.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can they stay hibernated over a long holiday? Yes, for up to 60 days. To keep one longer, start the hibernated instance, stop it, and start it again.
- Our instances run in an Auto Scaling group. Does that change the answer? Yes. You can't hibernate an instance in an Auto Scaling group. Use a warm pool with hibernated instances, which saves the RAM contents to the root volume.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
